source_text: Verumtamen utrum id, quod praeterierat, vel nunc intimet, expendendum est. Usque ad legem - inquit - peccatum in mundo [n104] . Tu dicis, quia hoc peccatum Apostolus naturale voluerit intellegi; quaero ergo, si usque ad legem fuit, cur desierit esse post legem. Neque enim acquiesco, ut usque ad legem usque ad finem eius potius quam usque ad exortum intellegam; mecum facit verbi proprietas: quod dicit usque ad legem fuisse, ostendit non esse post legem et, quodcumque tempore ablatum est, naturale non fuit. Quod ergo infregit censura legis et infringendo ex multa parte restinxit, imitatione apparet, non generatione susceptum.
pass_a_gloss: Nevertheless whether that which he had passed by he even now intimates is to be weighed. Until the law, he says, sin in the world. You say that the Apostle wanted this sin to be understood as natural; I ask therefore, if it was until the law, why it ceased to be after the law. For I do not acquiesce that I understand until the law as until its end rather than until its rising; the property of the word makes with me: what he says was until the law, he shows is not after the law, and whatever has been taken away by time was not natural. What therefore the censure of the law broke, and by breaking extinguished from a great part, appears taken up by imitation, not by generation.

lemmas.lexica: LS imitatio; Blaise moral copying vs generation of sin
LS generatio; Blaise vs imitatio in Rom 5:12
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS ratio; Blaise use of reason required for sin

pass_b_english: Nevertheless, we must consider whether he now at least intimates what he previously passed over. ‘Until the law,’ he says, ‘sin was in the world’ (Romans 5:13). You say the apostle intended this sin to be understood as natural. I therefore ask: if it existed until the law, why did it cease to exist after the law? I do not agree to understand ‘until the law’ as until its end rather than until its appearance. The expression’s proper meaning supports me: in saying it existed until the law, he shows it does not exist after the law. Anything removed in the course of time was not natural. Therefore what the law’s discipline broke, and in breaking largely extinguished, evidently arose through imitation, not generation.

choices.why: Julian's Rom 5:12 reading: sin passes by copying Adam's example, not by generation/seed.
Julian's target is Augustine's claim that sin is transmitted by begetting; keep generation vs imitation.
